title: Soils and slopes
subtitle: The ground beneath the vine
objectives: Explain what soil does for the vine
Describe the effect of drainage and heat retention

steps.title: What soil does
steps.body: Soil anchors the vine and supplies water and nutrients. The best vineyard soils are often poor, which limits vigour so the vine puts energy into fruit, not leaves. Drainage matters most: vines hate standing water, which suffocates roots and dilutes berries.

steps.title: Warm and cool soils
steps.body: Stony and gravel soils drain fast and store heat, releasing it at night, which helps ripening in cooler areas like the Médoc. Clay soils hold water and stay cool, which suits early-ripening grapes like Merlot. Dark slate in the Mosel absorbs warmth. Chalk drains well yet stores water deep, ideal for Champagne.

steps.prompt: Match each soil to its effect.
steps.explanation: Each soil changes water and heat around the roots, and so the ripening.

steps.title: Why slopes matter
steps.body: Slopes drain well and catch more sunlight when they face the sun: south or south-east in the northern hemisphere, north in the southern. Cold air flows downhill, so slopes avoid the frost that settles in valley floors. That's why Burgundy's best vineyards lie on the middle of the slope, and the Mosel's on steep south-facing banks.
steps.highlight: Slopes: drainage, sun and less frost

steps.prompt: Why are slopes often better vineyard sites than valley floors?
steps.explanation: Slopes drain, catch the sun and let cold air flow away. Valley floors usually have deeper, more fertile soils, which can lead to too much vigour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Poor, well-drained soils focus the vine on its fruit
Gravel and slate store heat; clay stays cool and wet
Slopes give drainage, sun and protection from frost
